questions.questionText: Prove by contradiction that √2 is irrational.
steps: 1. Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms with integers a, b and b ≠ 0. Then a² = 2b².
2. Thus a is even; write a = 2k. Substitution gives b² = 2k², so b is even.
3. Both a and b are even, contradicting that the fraction was in lowest terms.

questions.question: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many primes.
questions.questionText: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many primes.
questions.answer: The set of primes is infinite.
steps: 1. Assume the finite list p₁, …, pₙ contains every prime.
2. The integer N = p₁p₂…pₙ + 1 exceeds 1 and is not divisible by any listed prime.
3. N has a prime divisor outside the list, contradicting completeness.

questions.question: Prove by contradiction that √3 is irrational.
questions.questionText: Prove by contradiction that √3 is irrational.
steps: 1. Assume √3 = a/b in lowest terms, so a² = 3b².
2. An integer square divisible by 3 has its base divisible by 3. Write a = 3k; then b² = 3k², so 3 also divides b.

questions.question: Prove that no smallest positive real number exists.
questions.questionText: Prove that no smallest positive real number exists.
questions.answer: There is no smallest positive real number.
steps: 1. Assume r is the smallest positive real number.
2. Then r/2 is also a positive real number.

questions.question: In the √2 contradiction proof, why must a/b be in lowest terms?
questions.questionText: In the √2 contradiction proof, why must a/b be in lowest terms?
questions.answer: To make common evenness a contradiction.
steps: 1. If a and b were already allowed a common factor, both being even would cause no inconsistency.
2. Lowest terms rules out a common factor greater than 1.

questions.question: A contradiction argument starts by assuming its conclusion is true. What is wrong?
questions.questionText: A contradiction argument starts by assuming its conclusion is true. What is wrong?
questions.answer: It must assume the negation of the desired conclusion.
steps: 1. The aim is to show that the negation leads to an impossibility.
2. Assuming the result itself does not establish it.

questions.question: Prove that a rational number plus an irrational number is irrational.
questions.questionText: Prove that a rational number plus an irrational number is irrational.
steps: 1. If r + u were rational with rational r, then u = (r + u) - r would be rational.
2. That contradicts the assumption that u is irrational.

questions.questionText: Why does a contradiction proof of “all n have property P” start with an exception?
questions.answer: The negation is that at least one allowed n fails P.

questions.instruction: Answer the stated polynomial question.
steps: Step 1: Convert the divisor to its root. The divisor is x - 1, so set it equal to zero and get \(x=1\).
Step 2: Write the coefficients of \(P(x)=3x^{3} + x^{2} - x - 3\) in descending powers of \(x\). Include any zero coefficients if a power is missing.
Step 3: Carry out synthetic division: bring the first coefficient down, multiply by the root, then add down the next column.
Step 4: The final entry in the bottom row is the remainder. The other bottom-row entries are the quotient coefficients.
Step 5: Write the quotient with one lower degree than the original polynomial.
Because the remainder is 0, the divisor is a factor of the polynomial.

packs.title: Sampling and study design

questions.question: Critique the sampling plan. Give two limitations and one improvement.A survey asks, 'Do you agree that the excellent new park should stay open late?'
questions.questionText: Critique the sampling plan. Give two limitations and one improvement.A survey asks, 'Do you agree that the excellent new park should stay open late?'
questions.answer: Limitations should include question wording bias. Improvement: Use neutral wording, such as 'Should the new park stay open late?'
steps: A critique should refer to the target population, who is included, and who may be missed.
Limitation 1: The word 'excellent' pushes respondents towards a positive answer.
Limitation 2: the results may not generalise to the whole target population.

n(A ∩ B') = n(A) - n(A ∩ B) = 28 - 10 = 18.
This is A only: in A but not in B.

n(A' ∩ B) = n(B) - n(A ∩ B) = 31 - 10 = 21.
This is B only: in B but not in A.

n((A ∪ B)') = total - n(A ∪ B).
This means neither A nor B.

questions.question: A column-state Markov model has T = \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{10}\\\frac{1}{5} & \frac{7}{10}\end{matrix}\right]\) and initial state \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{1}{10}\\\frac{9}{10}\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the next state and the long-run state.
questions.questionText: A column-state Markov model has T = \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{10}\\\frac{1}{5} & \frac{7}{10}\end{matrix}\right]\) and initial state \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{1}{10}\\\frac{9}{10}\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the next state and the long-run state.
steps: Columns sum to 1; entry (i,j) is the probability of moving from j to i.
The next state is T times the initial column: \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{7}{20}\\\frac{13}{20}\end{matrix}\right]\).
For steady state let p + q = 1 and p = 0.8p + 0.3q. Thus 0.2p = 0.3q, so p = 0.6 and q = 0.4.
criteria: A1: Correct final value, units or interpretation [1].

questions.question: Given \(f\prime\prime(x)=(x-1)(x+1)\), find concavity intervals and candidate inflection inputs. Assume f is twice differentiable.
questions.questionText: Given \(f\prime\prime(x)=(x-1)(x+1)\), find concavity intervals and candidate inflection inputs. Assume f is twice differentiable.
questions.answer: Concave up outside [-1, 1], concave down between; inflections at -1 and 1.
steps: Step 1. The second derivative zeros are -1 and 1.
Step 2. Its signs on the resulting open intervals are positive, negative, positive.
Step 3. Each zero has a sign change, so each is an inflection input.

packs.title: Connected rates of change

questions.question: Lengths x and y vary with time t (s), with A = 3xy. At x = 2 cm, y = 5 cm, \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) = 4 cm/s and \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) = −1 cm/s, find \(\frac{dA}{dt}\).
questions.questionText: Lengths x and y vary with time t (s), with A = 3xy. At x = 2 cm, y = 5 cm, \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) = 4 cm/s and \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) = −1 cm/s, find \(\frac{dA}{dt}\).
steps:
Differentiate first [1] Both lengths change, so apply the product rule with respect to time.

\(\frac{dA}{dt}\) = 3(x \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) + y \(\frac{dx}{dt}\))

Substitute [1] Use the values at the stated instant only after differentiating.

\(\frac{dA}{dt}\) = 3(2(-1) + 5(4)) = 3(-2 + 20)

Simplify and interpret [1] The area quantity is increasing.

\(\frac{dA}{dt}\) = 54 cm²/s

questions.question: A square plate expands. When its side is 12 cm, its area increases at 48 cm²/s. Find the rate of increase of its side length.
questions.questionText: A square plate expands. When its side is 12 cm, its area increases at 48 cm²/s. Find the rate of increase of its side length.
steps:
Model [1] Let s(t) be the side length.

A = s²

Differentiate and substitute [1] Differentiate with respect to t before setting s = 12.

\(\frac{dA}{dt}\) = 2s \(\frac{ds}{dt}\); 48 = 24 \(\frac{ds}{dt}\)

Solve [1] The positive value indicates expansion.

\(\frac{ds}{dt}\) = \(\frac{48}{24}\) = 2 cm/s

questions.question: A spherical balloon has radius 6 cm increasing at 0.5 cm/s. Find its exact volume rate. Use \(V=\frac43\pi r^3\).
questions.questionText: A spherical balloon has radius 6 cm increasing at 0.5 cm/s. Find its exact volume rate. Use \(V=\frac43\pi r^3\).
steps:
Differentiate [1] The chain rule introduces the radius rate.

\(\frac{dV}{dt}\) = 4πr² \(\frac{dr}{dt}\)

Substitute [1] Insert the instantaneous radius and radius rate.

\(\frac{dV}{dt}\) = 4π(6²)(0.5)

Evaluate [1] Keep π for an exact answer; volume rate uses cubic units per second.

\(\frac{dV}{dt}\) = 72π cm³/s

questions.question: A 13 m ladder rests against a vertical wall. Its foot moves away at 0.6 m/s. When the foot is 5 m from the wall, find the signed rate and direction of the top.
questions.questionText: A 13 m ladder rests against a vertical wall. Its foot moves away at 0.6 m/s. When the foot is 5 m from the wall, find the signed rate and direction of the top.
questions.answer: \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) = -0.25 m/s; the top moves down at 0.25 m/s.
steps:
Model and snapshot [1] Let x be the foot’s distance from the wall and y the top’s height.

x² + y² = 13²; y² = 169 - 25 = 144; y = 12

Substitute and solve [1] The foot moves away, so its distance rate is positive.

10(0.6) + 24 \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) = 0; \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) = \(\frac{-6}{24}\) = -0.25
Interpret [1] Height is decreasing: the top moves down at 0.25 m/s.

questions.question: A vertex-down conical tank has height 10 m and top radius 5 m. Water enters at 3π m³/min. Find the depth rate at depth 6 m. Use \(V=\frac13\pi r^2h\).
questions.questionText: A vertex-down conical tank has height 10 m and top radius 5 m. Water enters at 3π m³/min. Find the depth rate at depth 6 m. Use \(V=\frac13\pi r^2h\).
steps:
Similar triangles [1] The water surface radius changes with depth.

\(\frac{r}{h}\) = \(\frac{5}{10}\) = \(\frac{1}{2}\); r = \(\frac{h}{2}\)

One-variable model [1] Substitute the radius-depth relationship before differentiating.

V = \(\frac{1}{3}\)π \(\frac{h²}{4}\) h = \(\frac{πh³}{12}\)

Substitute and solve [1] At h = 6, the coefficient is 9π.

3π = 9π \(\frac{dh}{dt}\); \(\frac{dh}{dt}\) = \(\frac{1}{3}\) m/min

questions.question: A balloon rises vertically at 2 m/s. An observer is 40 m from its launch point. Find the exact rate of its angle of elevation (radians) when its height is 30 m.
questions.questionText: A balloon rises vertically at 2 m/s. An observer is 40 m from its launch point. Find the exact rate of its angle of elevation (radians) when its height is 30 m.
steps:
Model [1] Let h be height. The horizontal distance remains fixed.

tan θ = \(\frac{h}{40}\)

Differentiate [1] Differentiate both sides with respect to time.

sec² θ \(\frac{dθ}{dt}\) = \(\frac{1}{40}\) \(\frac{dh}{dt}\)

Snapshot values [1] Use the height and fixed distance to find tan θ, then use sec² θ = 1 + tan² θ.

sec² θ = 1 + \(\frac{9}{16}\) = \(\frac{25}{16}\)

Solve [1] Use radians for the angular rate.

\(\frac{25}{16}\) \(\frac{dθ}{dt}\) = \(\frac{2}{40}\); \(\frac{dθ}{dt}\) = \(\frac{4}{125}\) rad/s

questions.question: A cylinder has fixed height 10 cm. Volume increases at 200π cm³/min. At r = 5 cm, find \(\frac{dr}{dt}\). Explain why inserting r = 5 before differentiating gives an incorrect zero rate.
questions.questionText: A cylinder has fixed height 10 cm. Volume increases at 200π cm³/min. At r = 5 cm, find \(\frac{dr}{dt}\). Explain why inserting r = 5 before differentiating gives an incorrect zero rate.
questions.answer: \(\frac{dr}{dt}\) = 2 cm/min. A snapshot radius cannot replace the changing radius before differentiation.
steps:
Model [1] The height is fixed but the radius is not.

V = 10πr²

Differentiate and substitute [1] Differentiate the changing relationship first.

\(\frac{dV}{dt}\) = 20πr \(\frac{dr}{dt}\); 200π = 100π \(\frac{dr}{dt}\)
Explain [1] The value 5 cm applies only at one instant. Substitution first erases the time dependence and produces a constant snapshot, not a volume function valid over time.

questions.question: A rectangle has constant area 96 m². At length 12 m and width 8 m, its length increases at 0.5 m/min. Find width and perimeter rates. Explain how perimeter changes while area stays fixed.
questions.questionText: A rectangle has constant area 96 m². At length 12 m and width 8 m, its length increases at 0.5 m/min. Find width and perimeter rates. Explain how perimeter changes while area stays fixed.
questions.answer: Width: -1/3 m/min; perimeter: 1/3 m/min. The width decreases as the length increases; constant area does not require constant perimeter.
steps:
Area relationship [1] Let L and w vary while their product remains fixed.

Lw = 96; L \(\frac{dw}{dt}\) + w \(\frac{dL}{dt}\) = 0

Width rate [1] Insert the snapshot dimensions.

12 \(\frac{dw}{dt}\) + 8(0.5) = 0; \(\frac{dw}{dt}\) = \(\frac{-1}{3}\) m/min

Perimeter rate [1] Add the signed length and width contributions.

\(\frac{dP}{dt}\) = 2(0.5) + 2(-\(\frac{1}{3}\)) = \(\frac{1}{3}\) m/min
Interpret [1] The width shrinks enough to hold the product Lw fixed. At these dimensions the sum L + w still increases, so the perimeter increases.

questions.question: Find \(\displaystyle \int \big(4x^{5} - 2x^{3} + 6x\big)\,dx\).
steps: Step 1: Use the reverse power rule on each term: add 1 to the power and divide by the new power.

Use the reverse power rule. Add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power.
$$\int ax^n\,dx=\dfrac{ax^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$$

For the term \(4x^{5}\), add 1 to the power.
$$5+1=6$$

Substitute into the reverse power rule.
$$\int 4x^{5}\,dx=\dfrac{4x^{6}}{6}$$

For the term \(-2x^{3}\), add 1 to the power.
$$3+1=4$$

Substitute into the reverse power rule.
$$\int -2x^{3}\,dx=\dfrac{-2x^{4}}{4}$$

For the term \(6x\), add 1 to the power.
$$1+1=2$$

Substitute into the reverse power rule.
$$\int 6x\,dx=\dfrac{6x^{2}}{2}$$
criteria: Correct reverse power rule and coefficients [1].
Correct combined antiderivative with integration constant [1].

questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{4} \big(-4x^{4} + 5x^{3} - 5x\big)\,dx\).
steps: Step 1: First find an antiderivative F(x), then evaluate F(upper limit) - F(lower limit).

Use the reverse power rule. Add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power.
$$\int ax^n\,dx=\dfrac{ax^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$$

For the term \(-4x^{4}\), add 1 to the power.
$$4+1=5$$

Substitute into the reverse power rule.
$$\int -4x^{4}\,dx=\dfrac{-4x^{5}}{5}$$

For the term \(5x^{3}\), add 1 to the power.
$$3+1=4$$

Substitute into the reverse power rule.
$$\int 5x^{3}\,dx=\dfrac{5x^{4}}{4}$$

For the term \(-5x\), add 1 to the power.
$$1+1=2$$

Substitute into the reverse power rule.
$$\int -5x\,dx=\dfrac{-5x^{2}}{2}$$

Subtract lower from upper; round at the end.
$$F(4)-F(0)\approx -539.200000-(0.000000)\approx -539.20$$

questions.questionText: Evaluate \(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{3} \big(-2x^{3} - 5x^{2}\big)\,dx\).
stepText: Step 1: First find an antiderivative F(x), then evaluate F(upper limit) - F(lower limit).

Use the reverse power rule. Add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power.
$$\int ax^n\,dx=\dfrac{ax^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$$

For the term \(-2x^{3}\), add 1 to the power.
$$3+1=4$$

Substitute into the reverse power rule.
$$\int -2x^{3}\,dx=\dfrac{-2x^{4}}{4}$$

For the term \(-5x^{2}\), add 1 to the power.
$$2+1=3$$

Substitute into the reverse power rule.
$$\int -5x^{2}\,dx=\dfrac{-5x^{3}}{3}$$

Subtract lower from upper; round at the end.
$$F(3)-F(0)\approx -85.500000-(0.000000)\approx -85.50$$

questions.questionText: For \(\dot x=1x,\quad\dot y=-y\) with (x(0), y(0)) = (1, 2), find the exact solution and classify the equilibrium at (0,0).
steps: \(\frac{dx}{x}=1\,dt,\quad\frac{dy}{y}=-dt\); integrate and use the initial conditions.
The eigenvalues are 1 and −1, with opposite signs. The origin is a saddle, unstable overall.
criteria: A1: Correct final value, units or interpretation [1].

questions.question: Use one simultaneous Euler step of h = 0.1 for \(\dot x=x-y,\quad\dot y=x+y\), starting at (x, y) = (1, 2).
questions.questionText: Use one simultaneous Euler step of h = 0.1 for \(\dot x=x-y,\quad\dot y=x+y\), starting at (x, y) = (1, 2).
steps: Evaluate both slopes at the old state (1, 2): \(\dot x=-1,\quad\dot y=3\).
\(y_1=2+0.1(3)=\frac{23}{10}\). Do not use the updated x in the y update.

questions.question: Solve \(\ddot x+1x=0\) with x(0) = 2 and \(\dot x(0)=0\).
questions.questionText: Solve \(\ddot x+1x=0\) with x(0) = 2 and \(\dot x(0)=0\).
steps: At t = 0, x = A = 2. Differentiate to obtain \(\dot x=-1A\sin(1t)+1B\cos(1t)\).
The initial velocity is zero, so B = 0. Substitute to check the differential equation.
